title: Using the ADAP Learning Algorithm to Forecast the Onset of Diabetes Mellitus
authors: Smith J.W., Everhart J.E., Dickson W.C., Knowler W.C., Johannes R.S.
venue: Proceedings of the Annual Symposium on Computer Application in Medical Care (Orlando, 7-11 Nov 1988), pp. 261-265
doi: NOT STATED (no DOI shown on the reference page)
evidence: METADATA-ONLY (the citation was verified on a reference-listing page; the facts about the study come from the UCI documentation file, read through a GitHub mirror; the original paper was not read)
dataset: Pima Indians Diabetes Database (this is the study that produced it): 768 patients
population: Women of Pima heritage, aged 21 or more, living near Phoenix, Arizona (UCI documentation)
models: ADAP learning algorithm (named in the title; details not read)
reported: 76 % sensitivity and 76 % specificity on the 192 test cases at a cutoff of 0.448 (UCI documentation text, not the paper)

learn: Cite this as the origin of the data and as the honest historical baseline (about 76 %). Read the paper itself before describing its method.

title: Diabetes mellitus prediction and diagnosis from a data preprocessing and machine learning perspective
authors: Chollette C. Olisah, Lyndon Smith, Melvyn Smith
venue: Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine 220, 106773
dataset: Pima Indian diabetes dataset (768 instances; 268 diabetic / 500 not) and the Laboratory of Medical City Hospital (LMCH) dataset (1000 instances)
population: Pima: women of Pima heritage; LMCH: hospital patients (details not recorded here)
preprocessing: Spearman-correlation feature selection; missing values handled by polynomial-regression imputation (the data are split into non-zero and zero sets; 7th-order polynomial)
missing: 'polynomial regression for missing value imputation' - zeros are treated as missing and predicted from the other values
balancing: NOT STATED on the page text read
models: Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and the authors' proposed Twice-Growth Deep Neural Network (2GDNN)
split: Train and test accuracy are both reported (split ratio not recorded here)
cv: 'grid search and repeated stratified k-fold cross-validation' (10 splits x 3 repeats)
reported: Pima, 2GDNN: train accuracy 99.01 %, test accuracy 97.25 %, precision 97.34 %, sensitivity 97.24 %, F1 97.26 %. The extraction also lists optimized RF as 99.02 % train and 100 % test accuracy. LMCH 2GDNN: 99.57 % train / 97.33 % test.
conclusions: The proposed 2GDNN with the proposed preprocessing beats RF and SVM on both datasets
limitations: NOT STATED on the page text read
flags: INFERENCE: 97-100 % test accuracy on Pima is far above every protocol-clean result in this guide (our 100 random splits: best accuracy 0.825). Such numbers need an explanation, not a copy. | The page does NOT say whether imputation and feature selection were fitted before or after the train/test split. This is an unresolved protocol question; it is NOT an accusation of leakage. | A perfect (100 %) test accuracy for one model on a 768-row, noisy medical table is itself a reason to read the methods section very carefully.
learn: Ask three questions of every high-accuracy paper: (1) was every learned step (imputation, scaling, feature selection, balancing) fitted on training rows only; (2) how many rows were in the test part; (3) is there an interval around the number. Imputing zeros by regression is an alternative design to our median-in-Pipeline; ours is simpler and leak-safe by construction.

title: A comparison of machine learning algorithms for diabetes prediction
authors: Jobeda Jamal Khanam, Simon Y. Foo
dataset: Pima Indian Diabetes (UCI): 768 patients, 699 instances after preprocessing (233 diabetic / 466 non-diabetic)
population: 'all the patients are female, and at least 21 years old'
preprocessing: Mean replacement of missing values; removal of outliers (45) and extreme values (26); Pearson-correlation feature selection; normalisation to 0-1
missing: 'We replaced the missing value with the corresponding mean value.' Missing counts given: Glucose 5, BP 35, SkinThickness 227, Insulin 374, BMI 11
features: Pearson correlation with cut-off 0.2: SkinThickness, BloodPressure and DPF removed; Glucose, BMI, Insulin, Pregnancies and Age kept
models: DT, KNN, RF, NB, AdaBoost, LR, SVM, plus neural networks with 1, 2 and 3 hidden layers
split: '85% train/test splitting method' (as extracted: read the paper to see which part is 85 %)
cv: K-fold cross-validation (K = 7 for KNN; 10-fold for the neural networks)
reported: Train/test split accuracy: LR 78.85 %, SVM 77.71 %, KNN 79.42 %, NB 78.28 %, RF 77.14 %, AdaBoost 79.42 %, DT 73.14 %. Neural network with 2 hidden layers, 400 epochs, learning rate 0.01: 88.6 % (Table 8: 88.57 %).
conclusions: 'the NN with two hidden layers is considered the most efficient and promising'
flags: The page does NOT say whether mean imputation, outlier removal, feature selection and scaling were fitted before or after the split. | INFERENCE: removing 'outliers' and 'extreme values' from the whole table before splitting also removes hard cases from the test part, which makes the test easier. The counts as extracted (45 + 26 = 71) do not add up to the 69 rows removed (768 - 699) - re-read the paper before quoting them. | The classical models land at 73-79 %, the same range as our measured 0.71-0.77; only the neural network claims 88.6 %.
learn: Good evidence that sensible classical models cluster around 77-79 % accuracy on this dataset. The 88.6 % figure should be treated as a claim to verify, not a target to copy. Their zero handling (mean) is one of the alternatives we tested in the zero-rule experiment (it changes AUC by under 0.01).

title: An ensemble approach for classification and prediction of diabetes mellitus using soft voting classifier
authors: Saloni Kumari, Deepika Kumar, Mamta Mittal
venue: International Journal of Cognitive Computing in Engineering 2, 40-46
evidence: PARTIAL (abstract and article content visible; full PDF behind access restrictions)
dataset: Pima Indians Diabetes (768 rows: 500 non-diabetic / 268 diabetic) and a Breast Cancer dataset
preprocessing: Min-max normalisation to [0,1]; label encoding of the outcome
missing: 'pregnancy attribute has 111, insulin attribute has 374, and skin thickness attribute has 227 missing values. All the missing values were replaced by the median for a particular attribute.' (quoted from the extraction)
models: Soft-voting ensemble of Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes and Random Forest; compared with KNN, SVM, DT, AdaBoost, Bagging, GradientBoost, XGBoost, CatBoost
split: 'divided into testing and training datasets with 20% and 70%' (as written - the numbers do not add to 100 %)
reported: Pima, soft voting: accuracy 79.08 %, precision 73.13 %, recall 70 %, F1 71.56 %, AUC 80.98 %. Breast cancer: accuracy 97.27 % in the table versus 97.02 % in the text.
conclusions: The soft-voting ensemble of RF, LR and NB 'gives 79.08% accurate results on the Pima Indians diabetes dataset'
flags: SOURCE FACT: the paper counts the 111 zero Pregnancies as 'missing' and replaces them by the median. Zero pregnancies is a valid value; Glucose, BloodPressure, SkinThickness, Insulin and BMI are the columns where zero is impossible. | The 20 % / 70 % split is an internal inconsistency in the text. | Whether preprocessing was fitted before or after the split is NOT STATED.
learn: Closest published precedent for OUR choice of three base models (Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Random Forest). Their Pima AUC 0.8098 sits inside our measured range (0.74-0.88 on one split; mean 0.82-0.84 over 100 splits). Their handling of Pregnancies is the mistake our viva question 'zero pregnancies vs zero glucose' is designed to catch.

title: Predicting Diabetes Mellitus With Machine Learning Techniques
authors: Quan Zou, Kaiyang Qu, Yamei Luo, Dehui Yin, Ying Ju, Hua Tang
dataset: Hospital physical-examination data from Luzhou, China (14 attributes, a large imbalanced set) and the Pima Indians dataset (8 attributes)
population: Luzhou: hospital check-up patients; Pima: women of Pima heritage aged 21+
preprocessing: 'We deleted the abnormal and missing samples'; PCA (SPSS) and mRMR for feature reduction
missing: Rows with missing/abnormal values deleted (complete-case analysis): Pima reduced to 392 rows
balancing: 'Due to the data unbalance, we randomly extracted 5 times data. And the result is the average of these five experiments.'
features: PCA (3 components for Pima) and mRMR (Pima: glucose, 2-h serum insulin, age)
models: Decision tree (J48 in WEKA), Random Forest (WEKA), neural network (MATLAB)
split: Independent test of 13,700 Luzhou samples for selected methods
cv: 5-fold cross-validation for the main comparison; 10-fold for the Pima comparison
metrics: Sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC)
reported: Pima, 5-fold, all features: RF ACC 0.7604, J48 0.7275, NN 0.7667. Pima, mRMR (3 features): RF 0.7721. Pima, 10-fold: mRMR+RF 0.7852, mRMR+J48 0.7806, all-features RF 0.7604, J48 0.7275. Luzhou independent test: all-features RF ACC 0.8963.
conclusions: 'finding suitable attributes, classifier and data mining method are very important'; fasting glucose is the most important single index
limitations: 'we cannot predict the type of diabetes' (only stated limitation)
flags: The extraction printed the raw Pima count as 786 (almost certainly a typo for 768); the 392 complete-case rows match our own count. | Whether preprocessing was fitted before or after the splits is NOT STATED.
learn: Shows the other defensible way to treat the zeros: delete incomplete rows (392 of 768). We keep all rows and impute, because deleting 49 % of the data costs more than imputation does (our zero-rule experiment). Their Pima accuracies of 0.73-0.79 agree with ours.

title: Prediction of Diabetes using Classification Algorithms
dataset: Pima Indians Diabetes Database (UCI): 768 instances, 8 attributes
models: Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, Decision Tree
metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, ROC area
reported: Naive Bayes: accuracy 76.30 %, precision 0.759, recall 0.763, F-measure 0.760, ROC area 0.819. SVM: accuracy 65.10 %, precision 0.424, recall 0.651, F 0.513, ROC area 0.500. Decision tree: accuracy 73.82 %, ROC area 0.751.
conclusions: 'Naive Bayes classification algorithm outperforms comparatively other algorithms ... with an accuracy of 76.30%'
flags: INFERENCE from simple arithmetic: 500 / 768 = 65.10 %, so the SVM's accuracy equals the share of the majority class and its ROC area is exactly 0.500 - it behaved like a classifier that says 'no diabetes' for everyone. Accuracy alone hides this; the ROC area exposes it.
learn: Honest, modest, and consistent with ours (NB accuracy about 0.76, ROC area 0.82). Supports keeping Gaussian Naive Bayes in the comparison, and is a ready-made example for the viva: always compare accuracy with the majority-class baseline (65.1 %) and always report AUC.

title: Optimizing diabetes classification with a machine learning-based framework
authors: Xin Feng, Yihuai Cai, Ruihao Xin
dataset: Pima (768 patients: 268 diabetic / 500 not) and 13 GEO gene-expression datasets (GPL570 platform)
preprocessing: Joint mean/median filling of missing values; IQR 'capping' of outliers (found better than removing them); SMOTEENN resampling
missing: 'mean and median joint filling method' for Glucose, BloodPressure, SkinThickness, Insulin and BMI; Pregnancies excluded because 0 values are 'reasonable'
balancing: SMOTEENN (SMOTE + Edited Nearest Neighbours), applied 'post-preprocessing, pre-training' (their Figure 8)
features: Logistic regression used to find significant features: Pregnancies, Glucose, BMI, DiabetesPedigreeFunction
models: Proposed DCSGAN, CNN, DNN, SVM, Naive Bayes, KNN, Decision Tree
cv: 'tenfold cross-validation ... dataset divided into 10 disjoint subsets, one used as validation, remaining nine for training'
reported: Pima: binary accuracy 96.27 %, precision = recall = F1 = 0.9698, AUC 0.9702; tertiary-classification accuracy 99.31 %
conclusions: 'framework proposed in this paper can accurately classify diabetes'
limitations: NOT STATED (no limitations section; future directions only)
flags: SOURCE FACT: handles the Pregnancies zeros correctly (kept as valid) - the same decision as ours. | NOT STATED whether SMOTEENN was applied inside each cross-validation training fold or to the whole table first. If it was applied to the whole table before partitioning, that is the over-sampling-before-splitting flaw measured by Vandewiele et al. (our own 'oversample before split' experiment: Random Forest AUC 0.83 -> 0.94). | No hold-out test set and no interval are reported.
learn: Shows the same zero logic as ours and a very high AUC. The right reaction is neither to copy nor to dismiss: ask whether resampling happened inside the folds. In our project nothing is resampled at all, which removes this whole class of error.

title: Robust diabetic prediction using ensemble machine learning models with synthetic minority over-sampling technique
authors: Pradeepa Sampath, Gurupriya Elangovan, Kaaveya Ravichandran, Vimal Shanmuganathan, Subbulakshmi Pasupathi, Tulika Chakrabarti, Prasun Chakrabarti, Martin Margala
dataset: Pima Indians Diabetes (obtained from Kaggle): 768 records (268 / 500)
population: Females over 21 of Pima ancestry near Phoenix, Arizona

missing: 'the missing values are imputed with the mean of the data'
balancing: SMOTE ('both the classes diabetes and non-diabetes seem to be balanced')
models: k-NN, Naive Bayes, Decision Tree, Random Forest, AdaBoost, XGBoost, and an AdaBoost + XGBoost ensemble

title: Predicting and classifying type 2 diabetes using a transparent ensemble model combining random forest, k-nearest neighbor, and neural networks
authors: Niloufar Zaferani, Mohammad Reza Afrash, Khadijeh Moulaei
dataset: Pima Indians Diabetes database: 768 samples, 8 features, used with THREE classes (Normal 23.57 %, Pre-diabetes 35.68 %, Diabetes 40.76 %)
population: Pima Indians (limitations paragraph: small, limited diversity)
preprocessing: Zero values replaced by feature means; min-max scaling; Spearman feature selection (p <= 0.0001 with Bonferroni correction)
missing: 'replacing these zero values with the mean of each feature'
balancing: NOT STATED whether applied before or after the split
features: Spearman rank correlation; kept Glucose, blood pressure, BMI, age, insulin
models: Random Forest, KNN, neural network; stacking with a logistic-regression meta-learner; weighted soft voting
cv: 'Nested cross-validation (5 outer and 5 inner folds) was applied to prevent data leakage'; preprocessing 'fit exclusively on the training portion of each fold'
metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1, AUROC, Brier score, expected calibration error; bootstrap 95 % intervals; paired t-tests and Wilcoxon tests
reported: Stacking ensemble, class 0: accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 and AUROC all 100 %; Random Forest 100 % for classes 0 and 2; KNN class 0 F1 83.3 %
conclusions: 'The stacking model achieved perfect performance and superior calibration'; LIME and SHAP identified glucose, BMI and blood pressure as key factors
limitations: 'relatively small size, insufficient diversity in features and sample population'
flags: SOURCE FACT: the paper uses three classes, but the original Pima label is binary (268 / 500). The three-class labels must have been created by the authors. | INFERENCE (to be checked in the methods section): the SHAP/LIME finding that the Normal-to-Prediabetes boundary lies at 100-125 mg/dL matches the fasting-glucose prediabetes range, and the Pima Glucose column is a 2-hour OGTT value. If the three classes were derived from glucose cut-offs, perfect scores are expected and say nothing about prediction (label leakage from a feature). | Strong protocol wording (nested CV, fit inside folds) does not by itself remove a label that is built from a feature.
learn: A model-answer for the question 'where does the label come from?'. Excellent protocol vocabulary to borrow (nested CV, preprocessing fitted inside folds, bootstrap intervals, calibration), but a 100 % score is a warning sign, not a result to match.

title: Towards Transparent Diabetes Prediction: Combining AutoML and Explainable AI for Improved Clinical Insights
authors: Raza Hasan, Vishal Dattana, Salman Mahmood, Saqib Hussain
dataset: Pima Indian Diabetes (primary; size not stated on the page), plus the scikit-learn diabetes dataset and a rural African-American patients dataset for generalisation
population: Pima primarily; other groups for generalisation
preprocessing: Standardisation; categorical encoding where needed; median imputation; data augmentation ('synthetic examples were generated for underrepresented classes')
missing: 'Missing values in critical features (Blood Pressure, Skin Thickness, Insulin) were imputed using median values from their respective columns.'
balancing: Synthetic examples for under-represented classes; timing relative to the split NOT STATED
models: AutoGluon (best_quality preset, 600 s) stacked ensembles of Random Forest, CatBoost, LightGBM, XGBoost and neural networks; a separate neural network (64-32-16)
metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, balanced accuracy, ROC-AUC, MCC, sensitivity, specificity
reported: Pima test set: accuracy 76.62 %, balanced accuracy 74.95 %, ROC-AUC 0.774, MCC 0.495, sensitivity 78.8 %, specificity 69.1 %; cross-validation mean accuracy 76.08 %. SHAP mean values: Glucose 0.25, BMI 0.18, DiabetesPedigreeFunction 0.12, Age 0.09.
conclusions: AutoML plus XAI (SHAP, LIME, Integrated Gradients, attention, counterfactuals) is 'both interpretable and practical'; an interactive Streamlit application lets clinicians explore predictions
limitations: Pima is one ethnic group; SHAP and LIME may miss complex interactions; false-positive rate could be lower; short AutoGluon time budget; no socio-economic or lifestyle features
flags: The generalisation datasets are not comparable to Pima (different features), so the 85 % 'average accuracy' mixes unlike tasks.
learn: The closest published design to ours (80:20 split, 5-fold stratified CV, SHAP, Streamlit, median imputation) and its numbers are modest and realistic (accuracy 0.77, AUC 0.77). Its top SHAP features (Glucose, BMI, DPF, Age) match ours. Where we differ: we keep one explainer done properly, test additivity, and report intervals.

title: Current Techniques for Diabetes Prediction: Review and Case Study
authors: Souad Larabi-Marie-Sainte, Linah Aburahmah, Rana Almohaini, Tanzila Saba
dataset: Review of 40+ studies (2013-2019) plus a case study on Pima (768 instances: 500 / 268)
preprocessing: Case study in Weka: values normalised to 0-1 and standardised to mean 0, SD 1
missing: 'missing values were replaced with the average value of the related attribute'
models: Case study: REPTree, M5P, OneR, PART, ZeroR, SMO, BayesNet, KStar (rarely used classifiers)
metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F-measure, ROC area, RMSE
reported: Case study: best accuracy REPTree 74.48 %; all classifiers 68 %-74 %. Review: deep-learning studies up to 95.1 % (CNN-LSTM).
conclusions: Recommends using these classifiers and developing combined models
limitations: None explicitly identified in the text read
flags: The reviewed 95.1 % figures come from other authors' protocols and are not comparable without their details.
learn: Another independent data point that ordinary classifiers reach 68-77 % accuracy under cross-validation on Pima. Useful in the introduction for 'what is the state of the art'.

title: Machine Learning and Data Mining Methods in Diabetes Research
authors: Ioannis Kavakiotis, Olga Tsave, Athanasios Salifoglou, Nicos Maglaveras, Ioannis Vlahavas, Ioanna Chouvarda
venue: Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal 15, 104-116 (PMID 28138367, PMCID PMC5257026)

authors: Mahreen Kiran, Ying Xie, Nasreen Anjum, Graham Ball, Barbara Pierscionek, Duncan Russell

authors: Sandip Kumar Singh Modak, Vijay Kumar Jha
